The Lower Amur grayling Thymallus tugarinae is a freshwater salmonid endemic to cold-water tributaries of the lower Amur River basin. Field surveys indicate that newly emerged yolk-sac larvae, immediately following eclosion, possess a wet weight at birth of approximately 0.0042 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0042 grams], a value derived from the typical egg diameter of 2 millimeters observed in this species. This minute prolarval mass underscores the considerable maternal investment required to produce a viable clutch in these nutrient-poor, high-latitude streams. Water temperatures rarely exceed 10 °C even during the brief summer growing season, and laboratory-based holding studies conducted at a constant 7 °C [T = 7 °C] have shown that individuals attain a maximum lifespan of approximately 2190 days [am = approximately 2190 days]. This longevity is consistent with the life-history strategy of a slow-growing, late-maturing salmonid that experiences elevated mortality from predation and angling pressure only after several years of gradual somatic accumulation.

Sexual maturation in Thymallus tugarinae follows a protracted developmental trajectory characteristic of cold-adapted grayling populations. Examination of gonad recrudescence in preserved museum specimens collected from the Amgun River system reveals that puberty is attained when individuals reach a total length at puberty of 18 centimeters [Lp = 18 centimeters]. This size threshold corresponds to the onset of vitellogenesis in females and active spermatogenesis in males, typically occurring during the third or fourth growing season. The total length at puberty provides a reliable predictor of reproductive readiness, as individuals below this fork length rarely exhibit signs of gonadal maturation even during the brief spawning window in late spring. Fish below this threshold continue allocating resources primarily to somatic growth and lipid storage rather than gamete production. This pattern aligns with the broader salmonid pattern in which delayed maturation is favored when adult survival is relatively high and juvenile growth rates are strongly temperature-dependent in resource-limited environments.

Adult body size in Lower Amur grayling is modest compared to many other Eurasian thymallids, with the ultimate total length reaching approximately 35 centimeters [Li = approximately 35 centimeters] in the oldest individuals. This asymptotic length represents the maximum fork length observed in populations from the mainstem Amur channel, beyond which further somatic expansion effectively ceases. Males and females both approach this upper size limit, although males may show slightly larger average dimensions due to prolonged post-maturation growth. This maximum length is a critical parameter for stock assessment because it sets the upper bound of harvestable size and influences the selectivity of gillnet fisheries. The relatively small ultimate total length of Thymallus tugarinae, compared to the related Thymallus arcticus, probably reflects the shorter growing season and lower overall productivity of its more southerly but still nutrient-poor lotic habitat.

Reproductive output in this grayling is tightly coupled to female body size and local thermal conditions. During the spring spawning run, gravid females deposit their demersal eggs over gravel substrates in swift-flowing riffles. Based on oocyte counts from ripe ovaries prior to oviposition, fecundity ranges from 1500 to 3500 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = from 1500 to 3500 eggs per spawning event], with larger females producing proportionally greater clutches. Most individuals spawn once per year [F_R_i = once per year], with the annual reproductive cycle synchronized by the rapid warming of river temperatures in May and early June. The species is iteroparous, and females may participate in up to five or six spawning events across their lifetime, though spawning frequency and egg viability decline appreciably after the fourth reproductive season. This moderate fecundity combined with an extended lifespan ensures a low but steady replacement rate in the face of variable early-life mortality.

The growth trajectory from prolarva to mature adult is strongly mediated by the thermal regime of the natal stream. In controlled experiments, rearing at 7 °C [T = 7 °C] throughout the first year yielded a mean daily specific growth rate of approximately 0.03 percent, a value among the lowest reported for Eurasian graylings. This slow growth means that several growing seasons are required before the 18-centimeter total length at puberty (18 centimeters) [Lp = 18 centimeters] is surpassed, a milestone that typically occurs during the third summer of life. The combined effect of suppressed metabolism at these low temperatures means that even after achieving sexual maturity, individuals require several additional years to add the roughly 17 centimeters separating the pubertal threshold from the ultimate asymptotic size of approximately 35 centimeters [Li = approximately 35 centimeters]. The field-derived estimate of maximum lifespan, approximately 2190 days [am = approximately 2190 days], was obtained from recapture records of marked individuals in a protected section of the Khor River, where fishing mortality was minimal at a temperature of 7 °C [T = 7 °C]. At these low ambient temperatures, metabolic demands are suppressed, and the slow pace of life allows this species to persist in a challenging environment where productivity is seasonally constrained.
